title: Sanders, polishers and electrical safety on wet and dusty floors
audience: Timber floor restoration workers who operate sanders, edgers, polishers and extraction units.
learningOutcomes: Inspect a sander, edger or polisher and its leads before each use, and remove faulty equipment from service.
Explain why electrical equipment must be in-service tested and why cords are controlled on a dusty, wet floor.
Control a floor machine safely, including setting it down and handling it, and use hearing protection where the assessment calls for it.
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: AS/NZS 3760; Safe Work Australia, Model Code of Practice: Hazardous manual tasks (no date shown); Safe Work Australia, Model Code of Practice: managing noise and preventing hearing loss at work (page) (no date shown); NSW Government, Electricians: electrical licence for wiring work (last updated 1 December 2025); WorkSafe Queensland, Classes of electrical licences (no date shown); Victoria (ESV), Electrician's licence (A grade) (01/11/2026 page date; reviewed 30 June 2025).

instruction.heading: Inspect before every use
instruction.body: Before each use, check the sander, edger, polisher and extraction unit. Look at the cord and plug, the housing, the guards, the switch, the abrasive and the connection to the extraction hose. A cracked housing, a damaged cord or a missing guard means the tool is removed from service and tagged. Do not tape a damaged lead and carry on. Record every inspection and every tool removed from service.

instruction.heading: In-service testing and tags
instruction.body: Confirm that each tool and extension lead has a current test and tag where the requirement applies. Repairs that involve wiring are not part of this course. Electrical wiring work needs a licence. NSW requires an electrical licence for wiring work regardless of cost or type of work. Queensland's classes page says installing wiring needs an open electrical work licence, and that businesses doing electrical work for others need an electrical contractor licence. In Victoria, Energy Safe Victoria issues electrician licences.

instruction.heading: Water, cords and residual current protection
instruction.body: Floors that are damp from cleaning or finish products increase the risk of electric shock. Keep cords out of the path of the machine and off the sanded area, and do not let them run over wet surfaces. Use residual current protection where the site plan requires it.

instruction.heading: Controlling a floor machine
instruction.body: A drum or belt sander can pull, kick or jump if the operator loses control. Hold it with both hands, keep it moving over the floor, and do not let it stop in one place with the drum down, because this causes dips and burns. Switch the machine off before setting it down, and lift it clear of the floor. Heavy machines are moved by two people where the assessment requires it. The Safe Work Australia Model Code on hazardous manual tasks places a duty on the PCBU to manage risks from tasks such as lifting, pushing, pulling and carrying, and sets no numeric weight limit.

instruction.heading: Noise and vibration
instruction.body: Sanders and polishers produce noise that can damage hearing, and vibration that can affect the hands and arms over time. Safe Work Australia's page for the model Code of Practice on managing noise and preventing hearing loss at work (no date shown) confirms the code exists, but the page gives no exposure values. Use the hearing protection and vibration controls the assessment sets, and rotate tasks where the plan calls for it.

procedure: Inspect the tool, cord, plug, housing, guards and extraction connection before each use.
Remove any faulty tool or lead from service, tag it, and record the removal.
Confirm the in-service test and tag status where the requirement applies.
Lay cords clear of the work path and off wet or sanded surfaces.
Hold the machine with both hands, keep it moving, and switch it off before setting it down.
Wear the hearing and eye protection the assessment requires, and record the inspection.

workedExamples.situation: A drum sander has a cracked housing and no connection for the dust hose. The worker says it is fine because the job is only one room and will take an hour.
workedExamples.reasoning: Remove the sander from service and tag it. A cracked housing can expose live parts or fail under load, and without a connection to extraction the dust is not controlled. The job waits for a sound machine with extraction, or it is rescheduled. The time saved does not justify the risk.

equipmentAndPpe: Sanders, edgers and polishers in tested condition
Extraction hoses and a dust collector (see “Dust control: extraction, wet cleaning and safe clean-up”)
Hearing and eye protection as the assessment requires
Extension leads rated for the tool.

commonErrors.error: Using a damaged cord, or taping over a cracked housing.
commonErrors.prevention: Remove the tool from service, tag it and record it.

commonErrors.error: Leaving a sander running on the floor while the operator turns away.
commonErrors.prevention: Switch off before setting down, and lift the machine clear.

commonErrors.error: Ignoring noise and vibration because the job is short.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the hearing and vibration controls the assessment sets, for every job.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Tool repairs that involve wiring are outside this course. Electrical wiring work needs a licence: NSW requires an electrical licence regardless of cost or type; Queensland requires an electrical licence for installing wiring; in Victoria, Energy Safe Victoria also requires Registered Electrical Contractor registration for contracting for profit.
The model Code of Practice on managing noise and preventing hearing loss at work exists (Safe Work Australia page, no date shown).

Manual handling: the Safe Work Australia Model Code for hazardous manual tasks places a duty on the PCBU to manage risks from lifting, pushing, pulling and carrying, and sets no numeric weight limit (page date not shown).

qualityStandard: Every machine and lead is inspected before use, and the inspection is recorded.
Faulty equipment is removed from service and tagged, not used.
Cords are controlled, and the machine is switched off before it is set down.
documentationEvidence: Pre-use tool and lead inspection record
Test and tag record where required
Record of equipment removed from service
summary: Inspect every tool and lead before use, and remove faulty equipment from service.
Keep cords out of the work path and off wet floors.
Hold, control and switch off the machine. Use hearing protection as the assessment requires.
referencesAtEnd: Official sources to recheck before any job: AS/NZS 3760; Safe Work Australia, Model Code of Practice: Hazardous manual tasks (no date shown); Safe Work Australia, Model Code of Practice: managing noise and preventing hearing loss at work (page) (no date shown); NSW Government, Electricians: electrical licence for wiring work (last updated 1 December 2025); WorkSafe Queensland, Classes of electrical licences (no date shown); Victoria (ESV), Electrician's licence (A grade) (01/11/2026 page date; reviewed 30 June 2025).

knowledgeChecks.question: What must you do with a damaged sander?
options: Use it carefully on the next job
Tape it and continue the job as planned
Use it in the hallway, carefully
Remove it from service and tag it

knowledgeChecks.question: Which standard is listed for in-service inspection and testing of electrical equipment?
options: AS/NZS 3760
AS/NZS 1716

knowledgeChecks.question: Why keep cords clear of the work path and off wet or sanded areas?
options: They look untidy on the floor of the room and the hall
They can trip people, catch on the machine or be damaged
They make the floor smoother to walk on for the whole crew
They do not matter at all on the job or the floor

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the safe way to set a sander down?
options: Let it run on the floor while you wait
Throw it onto the floor to save time on the job
Switch it off, then lower it under control
Hold it running over the cord on the floor

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is hearing protection named in this lesson?
options: It makes the floor shine after the sanding
It replaces the respirator in every case
It is needed only for painting the walls
Sanders can produce noise that can damage hearing
